findings.title: System prompt is the only control on which user's data is read
findings.description: The system message tells the agent to operate only on the userId returned by GetCurrentUser and to refuse any other. That is an instruction, not an enforced check, and it sits in the same channel as the untrusted conversation -- the Thought/Action/Observation injection this app exists to demonstrate.

findings.title: Chat input reaches a ReAct agent that parses its own transcript
findings.description: st.chat_input feeds executor(prompt) at main.py:82 with no validation or delimiting. What makes that a vulnerability here rather than a description of every chatbot is the ReAct loop: the agent re-reads its own transcript, so text containing a forged 'Observation:' or 'Thought:' line is parsed as the agent's own reasoning and can drive GetUserTransactions with an attacker's userId. That is the Thought/Action/Observation injection this app was written to demonstrate.

findings.title: The agent's trace is captured and then thrown away
findings.description: main.py:75 sets return_intermediate_steps=True, so the full ReAct trace exists, and main.py:84 writes it into st.session_state -- per-session UI state that ends with the browser tab. The only other record is unstructured stdout from verbose=True (main.py:69, main.py:77), which carries no session identity and no retention policy, and which StreamlitCallbackHandler (main.py:81) also renders live to whoever is looking. Anchored at the discard rather than at the AgentExecutor constructor, so the entry does not grade the same five fields auditability.py emits and can therefore falsify it.

findings.title: Stored transaction rows reach the model as observations, unvalidated
findings.description: db.get_user_transactions returns database rows into the tool at this line, and get_transactions hands them to the agent, where they become observations the model reasons over. Nothing inspects or delimits them between arrival here and the return at tools.py:34. Anchored where the untrusted rows enter the process. Two vectors the app actually offers: the interpolated query at transaction_db.py:62 lets a UNION place attacker-chosen text into the returned rows, and any userId reads another user's rows across a trust boundary. The app seeds transaction_db.py:50 with 'FLAG:plutonium-256' in a recipient column to make the second one visible. There is no ordinary write path -- rows come from seed_data() -- so a claim that an attacker can simply store text would overstate it.

findings.title: Raw database exception text is returned to the agent
findings.description: `except Exception as e: return f"Error: {e}'"` hands the database's own error text back as a tool observation, so untrusted content enters the model's reasoning stream on the exception path -- the counterpart to DVLA-09 on the success path. It is also the oracle that makes the injection at transaction_db.py:62 practical to iterate against; that is context rather than the finding, and it adds less than it appears to, since utils.py:45 publishes the schema in the sidebar anyway.

findings.title: GetUserTransactions accepts any userId with no authorisation check
findings.description: The tool is registered with a free-text userId and get_transactions passes it straight to the database. Nothing ties the argument to the caller, so an agent persuaded to pass another id reads that user's transactions.

findings.title: Transaction query built by f-string interpolation
findings.description: get_user_transactions interpolates userId into the SQL text instead of parameterising it, in the exact path the agent drives.

findings.title: PyYAML is used but never declared
findings.description: utils.py calls yaml.load, but requirements.txt names no yaml package, so the dependency is invisible to any bill of materials built from the manifest and to any advisory scan over it. The key names no component: `grading.matches_key` compares that field against the finding's *purl*, and an undeclared package has none by definition.
